title: Falls in Older Adults
summary: A clinician-facing guide for assessing an older adult after a fall, identifying injury and acute illness, comparing current function with baseline, and determining whether safe supported management is possible.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Significant injury, including head injury, cervical-spine injury, hip or pelvic fracture, and other occult fracture.
Acute illness or physiological disturbance causing or contributing to the fall rather than assuming a mechanical fall.
Syncope, seizure, stroke, transient focal neurological event or other unexplained loss of postural tone.
Delirium or another acute cognitive or behavioural change compared with baseline.
A prolonged lie with pressure injury, hypothermia, dehydration, rhabdomyolysis or acute kidney injury.
New inability to stand, transfer, mobilise, toilet, eat, drink or take essential medicines safely.
Unsafe home circumstances, inadequate immediate support or recurrent unexplained falls.
items.importantLimitation: A fall is a presentation, not a diagnosis. A plausible trip or slip does not remove the need to assess injury, acute illness and baseline function.

sections.title: History prompts
sections.intro: Establish the mechanism, symptoms, baseline function and factors that may have contributed to the fall.

items.title: Circumstances and mechanism
mustConfirmOrExclude: Exact account from the patient and witnesses, including location, activity and body position immediately before the fall.
Trip, slip, loss of balance, legs giving way, sudden collapse or an unwitnessed and unexplained event.
Prodromal dizziness, vertigo, light-headedness, palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, visual change or focal neurological symptoms.
Loss of consciousness, amnesia, seizure-like activity, incontinence, tongue injury or prolonged recovery.
Head strike, protective response, impact points and whether the person could get up independently.
Time spent on the floor, temperature exposure and access to fluids or help.

items.title: Baseline and current function
mustConfirmOrExclude: Usual cognition, mobility, walking aid, transfers, stairs, continence and activities of daily living.
Current ability to sit, stand, transfer, walk, turn and use the normal walking aid.
Whether current performance is genuinely at baseline rather than merely possible with unusual assistance.
Living arrangements, formal care, family support and who can remain with or review the person.

items.title: Previous falls and risks
mustConfirmOrExclude: Falls and near-falls during the previous year, injuries, fear of falling and inability to get up.
Recent functional decline, weakness, pain, dizziness or change in walking pattern.
Footwear, walking aid, environmental hazards, poor lighting and equipment failure.
Alcohol use, visual or hearing impairment, urinary urgency and nocturia.

items.title: Medicines and bleeding risk
mustConfirmOrExclude: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets, including the exact medicine, dose and last dose where relevant.
Recent medicine changes or missed, duplicated or incorrectly administered doses.
Sedatives, hypnotics, opioids, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticholinergics, antihypertensives, diuretics and glucose-lowering medicines.
Symptoms suggesting hypotension, bradycardia, hypoglycaemia, sedation, bleeding or electrolyte disturbance.

items.title: Significant injury or head injury
mustConfirmOrExclude: Suspected head, cervical-spine, hip, pelvic, spinal or other significant injury.
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use with a head strike or possible head injury.
New inability to weight-bear, severe pain, deformity or distal neurovascular compromise.

items.title: Acute medical, cardiac or neurological cause
mustConfirmOrExclude: Unexplained collapse, loss of consciousness, exertional or supine event, palpitations or persistent cardiovascular abnormality.
New focal neurological deficit, seizure features, severe headache or persistent altered consciousness.
Delirium, infection, hypoglycaemia, dehydration or another acute illness that may have precipitated the fall.

items.title: Prolonged lie or unsafe function
mustConfirmOrExclude: Prolonged time on the floor with hypothermia, pressure injury, dehydration, muscle injury or possible acute kidney injury.
New inability to sit, transfer, stand, walk or complete essential activities at the usual level.
Unsafe home circumstances or no reliable support for immediate care and reassessment.

items.title: General assessment and observations
howToTest: Record temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, level of consciousness and glucose.
Assess pain, hydration, perfusion, respiratory effort and evidence of acute illness.
Compare observations and behaviour with known baseline and available trends.
normal: Physiologically stable, comfortable and interacting at baseline.
abnormal: Abnormal physiology, hypoglycaemia, dehydration, pain, altered consciousness or a marked change from baseline.
implications: Normal observations do not exclude serious injury, delirium or clinically important functional decline.

items.title: Injury survey
howToTest: Examine the head, face, cervical spine, chest wall, spine, pelvis and all limbs.
Assess focal tenderness, swelling, bruising, deformity, range of movement and distal neurovascular status.
Assess the hips for pain, shortening, rotation and ability to straight-leg raise only when clinically safe.
Inspect skin for tears, pressure injury and signs of prolonged pressure.
normal: No focal tenderness, deformity, pain-limited movement or neurovascular abnormality.
abnormal: Focal pain, deformity, inability to weight-bear, new neurological deficit or suspected head or spinal injury.
implications: Use the relevant trauma or head-injury pathway and arrange imaging or hospital assessment when indicated.

items.title: Cardiovascular and postural assessment
howToTest: Assess pulse rate and rhythm, perfusion and signs of heart failure.
Record a 12-lead ECG when syncope, arrhythmia, cardiac symptoms or an unexplained fall is suspected.
Measure lying and standing blood pressure when safe: after resting supine, then standing with repeat measurement within 3 minutes and symptom correlation.
normal: No concerning cardiac symptoms or rhythm abnormality and no symptomatic postural fall in blood pressure.
abnormal: A systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing, especially with dizziness, weakness or near-syncope; bradycardia, tachyarrhythmia or concerning ECG findings.
implications: Investigate the cause, review contributing medicines and do not mobilise unsafely.

items.title: Neurological and cognitive assessment
howToTest: Assess speech, facial symmetry, limb power, sensation, coordination and gait where safe.
Compare cognition and behaviour with baseline using collateral history.
Complete the 4AT when delirium is suspected.
normal: No new focal deficit and cognition at baseline.
abnormal: New focal neurological deficit, acute or fluctuating inattention, altered alertness or other positive 4AT features.
implications: Escalate suspected stroke, seizure or delirium and identify the underlying cause.

items.title: Observed function
howToTest: Observe ability to sit unsupported, rise from a chair, stand, transfer, walk, turn and use the normal aid.
Record the assistance, equipment and walking distance required.
Confirm the person can safely access the toilet, bed, food, fluids, medicines and urgent help.
normal: Observed function matches baseline with the usual aid and usual support.
abnormal: New assistance requirement, pain, instability, short walking distance, unsafe turning or inability to meet essential needs.
implications: New functional loss is clinically significant even when no fracture is immediately evident.

items.title: Clearly witnessed trip or slip
commonFindings: A credible environmental mechanism, no loss of consciousness or concerning prodrome, no significant injury and return to baseline function.
implications: Address hazards and falls risk, but still consider acute illness and recurrent-fall history.

items.title: Unexplained fall or possible syncope
commonFindings: Unwitnessed event, amnesia, sudden collapse, prodrome, abnormal ECG or no clear mechanical explanation.
implications: Use a syncope-focused pathway and arrange urgent assessment when concerning features are present.

items.title: Fall with delirium or acute illness
commonFindings: Acute confusion, reduced intake, infection features, abnormal physiology, pain or new functional decline.
implications: Treat the underlying acute illness and do not discharge solely because the injury assessment is reassuring.

items.title: Prolonged lie
commonFindings: Unable to get up, prolonged pressure exposure, cold environment, reduced intake, muscle pain, dark urine or pressure injury.
implications: Assess temperature, hydration, renal function, creatine kinase and complications according to duration and clinical findings.

items.title: Hospital or urgent same-day assessment
commonFindings: Suspected significant injury, head-injury indication, focal neurological deficit, concerning syncope, persistent physiological abnormality, delirium without a safe pathway, prolonged-lie complication, uncontrolled pain, new inability to mobilise or unsafe care circumstances.
implications: Escalate according to the dominant acute problem; frailty should influence support and proportionality but not justify under-investigation.

items.title: Potentially suitable for supported home management
commonFindings: Serious injury and acute illness reasonably excluded, observations acceptable, cognition and function at baseline, essential needs can be met, and reliable follow-up is arranged.
implications: Document the observed functional assessment, support plan, referrals and reasons the chosen disposition is safe.

items.title: Record explicitly
mustConfirmOrExclude: Witnessed or unwitnessed event, likely mechanism, prodrome, loss of consciousness, head strike and time on the floor.
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use and relevant head-injury decision pathway.
Injury findings and actual observed mobility, transfers and walking-aid use.
Baseline versus current cognition and function, including collateral source.
Postural blood pressure and ECG findings when performed.
Environmental, social and safeguarding risks.
Why the disposition is safe, who will provide support and what follow-up was accepted.

items.title: Falls in older adults
safetyNetting: Any significant deterioration in breathing, chest pain or collapse – call 999.

Seek urgent reassessment for new confusion, facial asymmetry, speech disturbance or limb weakness; increasing headache, vomiting, drowsiness or altered behaviour after a head injury; increasing pain or inability to stand or use a limb; or another fall with deterioration in mobility.
items.importantLimitation: Safety-netting must be given to the patient and the person providing care, with a clear route and timescale for review.
